transcript.content: Hi, it's good to meet you. What brings you in today?

I came in because… honestly, it’s this fear of flying. The thought of getting on an airplane now scares me so badly that I can’t really talk myself out of it. I know, in my head, it doesn’t make sense the way my body reacts, but it feels like the plane is going to fall. Like that’s what my body is telling me, even if I know logically that isn’t reasonable.
Is this fear only about flying?

It’s really about flying, yes. I mean, that’s the thing that brought me here. The thought of getting on an airplane now just scares me so badly that I can’t reason with it. I can tell myself it doesn’t make sense, I can know that logically, but my body reacts like the plane is going to fall. That’s the picture I get, or the feeling, like once I’m on it something terrible is going to happen. So yes, it’s specifically the airplane, the flying part.
Do these intense fear episodes ever happen when you are not flying or not thinking about flying?

Not really out of the blue, no. It’s tied to flying or something that makes me think I might have to fly.

Like, even if I’m not at an airport or anywhere near a plane, if I get an email about a rural shift that would require a flight, it hits immediately. I’ll just see the message come in and my heart starts pounding right away, my hands get sweaty, and I feel like I can’t get a full breath in. It’s almost ridiculous because I’m just sitting there looking at my inbox, but my body reacts like I’m already about to board. Sometimes I have to close the message just to calm down enough to keep going.
Did this fear of flying start after a frightening or traumatic experience on a plane?

Yes… I think that’s really when it started. It’s been about seven months now. There was this turbulent flight on a small plane, and it was right after I’d lost my clinic job, so I was already in a pretty bad place emotionally. The flight itself was rough enough that it really stuck with me, and after that it was like something changed. Since then, flying hasn’t felt like just an inconvenience or something I dislike — it’s become this thing I can’t get past.
Do you get unwanted memories or nightmares about that turbulent flight?

I don’t think so… not in the way you mean, I guess. I don’t really have nightmares where I’m back on that plane or anything like that. And I don’t sit around having these clear, unwanted memories of it playing like a movie.

It’s more that if flying comes up, I remember the feeling of it — the shaking, the sense that I couldn’t do anything — but I’m not sure I’d call that a flashback or an intrusive memory. It doesn’t just barge in when I’m doing something totally unrelated, at least not that I’ve noticed. It’s more connected to the idea of having to fly again.
Have you been avoiding flying since that turbulent flight?

Yes. Very much, honestly. Since that flight, I’ve been doing almost anything I can to not get on a plane.

I’ve canceled clinic coverage when it meant I’d have to fly out somewhere, even when I knew it caused problems for other people. I’ve skipped medical meetings I normally would have gone to, or at least tried to attend, because the thought of the airport and boarding was just… I couldn’t make myself do it.

And I’ve put off going to see my family in Honduras, which makes me feel awful. It’s not that I don’t want to see them. I do. I really do. But when it gets to the point of actually going to the airport, I just freeze up. If I have gone near it, I’m shaking, and I need someone with me, like I’m holding on to them just to get through it. It feels embarrassing to say that as a grown man, and as a doctor, but that’s what it’s been like.
When you get this fear around flying, is a big part of it that other people might notice your anxiety or judge you for it?

I’m not sure that’s the main thing, no. I mean… I do feel embarrassed sometimes, especially because I feel like I should be more composed, and I don’t like the idea of looking like I’m falling apart in public. But when the fear really hits, it isn’t mostly, “Oh no, people will see me shaking,” or “They’ll think badly of me.”

It’s more about the flying itself. The plane, being trapped there, the takeoff, the turbulence, the feeling that once I’m on it I can’t just get off if I need to. Other people noticing is uncomfortable, yes, but it feels secondary. If I could be completely alone and no one could see me, I think I’d still be just as afraid of getting on the plane.
Outside of anything related to flying, do you find yourself worrying excessively about a lot of other things in your life?

I don’t think so, no… at least not in the way this flying thing feels.

I mean, I’m a doctor, so there are always things to think about — patients, scheduling, family responsibilities, money here and there, normal adult life. I can overthink things like anyone else, especially if there’s a lot going on. But I wouldn’t say I’m constantly worrying about everything or jumping from one worry to another all day.

This feels much more… specific. Like, if flying isn’t on the horizon, I can generally function. I’m not sitting at home worrying excessively about ten different areas of my life for no reason. The fear really spikes when travel comes up, or when I imagine being on a plane. Outside of that, I don’t think I’m unusually anxious about lots of other things.
Since that turbulent flight, have you been feeling especially on guard or easily startled?

I’m not sure I’d describe it that way, no. I mean… I can feel tense when something reminds me of flying, but “on guard” all the time or jumping at every little sound — I haven’t really noticed that as a general thing.

When you say easily startled, do you mean like reacting to noises or people coming up behind me? Because I don’t think that’s been a big issue for me. I’m not walking around every day feeling like something is about to happen. At least, not outside of the flying situation.
Have you ever had one of these panic-like episodes come on suddenly when you were not thinking about flying or facing a flight?

I don’t think so… at least, I can’t really think of an example where it just came out of nowhere while I was, you know, doing something totally unrelated.

When I get that panicky feeling, it’s usually tied to flying in some way — like if I’m getting close to a flight, or I’m picturing the flight, or something makes me think about being on the plane. I might be going about my day and then remember, “Oh God, I have to fly,” and then my body can react pretty fast, but it doesn’t feel like it’s random exactly.

I haven’t noticed myself sitting at home calmly watching TV or seeing patients or walking down the street and suddenly having a full episode with no connection to that. If anything, there’s usually some trigger or thought about flying that I can trace it back to, even if it takes me a minute to realize that’s what set it off.
When these episodes happen, do they ever come completely out of the blue, without any trigger at all?

Not completely out of the blue, no. There’s usually something connected to flying, even if it’s small.

Like, it doesn’t even have to be an actual flight booked. If I get an email about a rural shift that would require me to fly, I can be sitting there totally fine, just going through messages, and the second I see it my heart starts pounding. My hands get sweaty almost immediately, and I get that tight, can’t-catch-my-breath feeling. It happens so fast that it feels sudden, but I can still point to the trigger.

Honestly, sometimes I just close the message because I feel like I can’t breathe properly while I’m looking at it. Once it’s off the screen, I can start to settle a bit. So it’s not random in the sense of coming from nowhere — it’s more that the reaction is immediate when something about flying shows up.
